title: Server-Handler Timing Reported as End-to-End Latency
pattern: Request latency is measured only between handler entry and exit on the server (`T3 - T2`) and reported as the system's request latency, omitting accept/socket queueing, network transit and response transmission (`T1 → T2`, `T3 → T4`).
why_bad: Queueing before the handler runs is where overload shows up first. A saturated server can report 1 ms handler latency while clients wait 500 ms in the kernel backlog or the runtime's accept queue, so dashboards and benchmarks stay green through the outage.
detection: A duration measured from handler entry to handler exit that is published or asserted as the overall request/response latency (metric names like `request_latency`, benchmark output labelled as latency), with no client-side (`T4 - T1`) measurement or queue-wait metric alongside it.
counterexample: Metrics explicitly named and used as service/processing time (e.g. `handler_cpu_time`) to isolate application execution from transport, reported next to client-observed latency.
source: Richard L. Sites, *Understanding Software Dynamics* (2021), Ch. 1, §1.4, p. 7; Ch. 6, §6.6, p. 92; Ch. 10, §10.3, p. 161.
